claims.text: Nearly equiatomic five-transition-metal HEA nanoparticles have intrinsic thermal stability and resistance to atomic diffusion at elevated temperatures.
High configurational entropy suppresses the thermodynamic driving force for phase separation and precipitation.
Severe lattice distortion caused by atomic-size mismatch kinetically inhibits precipitate nucleation and growth.
HEA nanoparticle behavior fundamentally deviates from traditional alloying because entropy is negligible and diffusion is rapid in traditional alloys.
CoCrFeMnNi or Al0.1CrCoFeNi nanoparticles can initially exist as single-phase fcc or bcc solid solutions.
The initial quinary solid solution has high chemical disorder.
Heating to 0.5–0.8 Tm or ion irradiation induces thermal activation and atomic mobility.
High configurational entropy and severe local lattice distortion or chemical short-range-order fluctuations act as barriers to atomic migration and phase nucleation.
Configurational entropy lowers the Gibbs free energy of the disordered solid solution relative to ordered or segregated phases.
Atomic-size mismatch creates deep potential-energy wells for diffusing atoms and thereby produces sluggish diffusion.
Sluggish diffusion kinetically restrains precipitate formation.
The combined thermodynamic and kinetic effects prevent precipitation under both thermal and irradiation stress.
The nanoparticles will show no observable phase separation or precipitation at elevated temperatures and will retain a single-phase solid solution.
The nanoparticles will exhibit no significant grain growth at elevated temperatures.
Traditional binary or ternary alloys rapidly precipitate secondary phases or decompose at elevated temperatures because they have low configurational entropy and rapid diffusion.
Significant deviation from equiatomic composition reduces configurational entropy and can invalidate the stability mechanism.
Insufficient atomic-size mismatch prevents severe lattice distortion and invalidates the proposed kinetic stabilization.
Above a critical temperature, the enthalpic driving force for ordering can overcome entropic stabilization.
At sufficiently small nanoparticle size, surface energy can dominate and induce phase separation.
Nanoparticle surface effects and finite-size constraints may alter diffusion pathways and phase stability relative to bulk HEAs.
